items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A system in which a hereditary monarch holds supreme power, not limited by a constitution or parliament"?
items.answer: absolute monarchy
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of absolute monarchy.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a constitutional monarchy and an absolute monarchy.
items.answer: In a constitutional monarchy the monarch's powers are limited by law and an elected parliament governs (UK, Japan); in an absolute monarchy the monarch holds supreme power (Saudi Arabia, Eswatini).
items.markingKey: In a constitutional monarchy the monarch's powers are limited by law and an elected parliament governs (UK, Japan); in an absolute monarchy the monarch holds supreme power (Saudi Arabia, Eswatini). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "A country with a monarch cannot be a democracy." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Constitutional monarchies such as Norway, Japan and the UK are democracies: elected parliaments hold power and the monarch's role is largely ceremonial.
items.markingKey: Constitutional monarchies such as Norway, Japan and the UK are democracies: elected parliaments hold power and the monarch's role is largely ceremonial. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A – Political philosophy (paraphrased): Paraphrase of John Locke, "Two Treatises of Government", 1689

The philosopher argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property. Governments are created by the consent of the people to protect these rights, and if a government abuses its power, the people have the right to change it.

Identify two points that Source A makes about why societies need rules and laws, and types of government, using evidence from the source.
items.answer: Government should protect natural rights and depends on the consent of the governed.
items.markingKey: Government should protect natural rights and depends on the consent of the governed. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [2]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Switzerland's referendums shows direct democracy in a modern state.
items.answer: Swiss citizens vote several times a year on national, cantonal and local issues, and can force a referendum with 50 000 signatures. A modern state can combine representative and direct democracy.
items.markingKey: Context (Swiss citizens vote several times a year on national, cantonal and local issues, and can force a referendum with 50 000 signatures.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a modern state can combine representative and direct democracy. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to direct democracy in a modern state.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Democracy is always the best form of government."
items.answer: Democracy is the system most likely to protect rights and accountability, but it works well only with the rule of law, protected minorities and informed citizens.
items.markingKey: From the source: Government should protect natural rights and depends on the consent of the governed. Own knowledge for: it protects rights and lets citizens remove leaders peacefully; leaders are accountable through elections and free media. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "rule of law".
items.answer: The principle that everyone, including leaders, is subject to the same laws, applied fairly by independent courts
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the principle that everyone, including leaders, is subject to the same laws, applied fairly by independent courts. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why societies need rules and laws.
items.answer: Laws keep order and protect people's safety, rights and property, settle disputes peacefully, and make expectations clear so people can cooperate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Laws keep order and protect people's safety, rights and property, settle disputes peacefully, and make expectations clear so people can cooperate. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Laws and rules are the same thing." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Rules can be set by any group (a school, a club); laws are made by the state and enforced by courts and police.
items.markingKey: Rules can be set by any group (a school, a club); laws are made by the state and enforced by courts and police. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: Liberals 4, Farmers' Party 1, Greens 1

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "India's constitution has been successful in protecting democracy." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Largely successful: democratic institutions have survived and adapted, though the Emergency and ongoing inequality show that rights depend on vigilant citizens and courts.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: regular elections and peaceful transfers of power since 1952; courts have protected the basic structure and rights. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Directive Principles of State Policy"?
options: A legally recognised member of a state, with rights and responsibilities
Guidelines in Part IV of the Constitution for governments to follow in making policies, which are not enforceable in courts
A system of government in which power comes from the people, who choose their leaders in free and fair elections
To formally approve a treaty so that a country agrees to be legally bound by it
items.answer: Guidelines in Part IV of the Constitution for governments to follow in making policies, which are not enforceable in courts
items.markingKey: B. "Directive Principles of State Policy" is guidelines in Part IV of the Constitution for governments to follow in making policies, which are not enforceable in courts.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Fundamental Rights are enforceable in court but Directive Principles are not.
items.answer: Fundamental Rights protect individuals from the state and can be claimed immediately; Directive Principles are goals (e.g. living wages, health) that depend on resources, so they guide policy rather than give legal claims.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Fundamental Rights protect individuals from the state and can be claimed immediately; Directive Principles are goals (e.g. living wages, health) that depend on resources, so they guide policy rather than give legal claims. items.stem: Explain the difference between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy.
items.answer: Fundamental Rights (Part III) are individual rights enforceable in court, such as equality and freedom of speech; Directive Principles (Part IV) are non-enforceable goals for government policy, such as equal pay and free education.
items.markingKey: Fundamental Rights (Part III) are individual rights enforceable in court, such as equality and freedom of speech; Directive Principles (Part IV) are non-enforceable goals for government policy, such as equal pay and free education. items.stem: Outline one way in which Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) shows the role of courts in protecting the Constitution.
items.answer: The Supreme Court ruled that Parliament can amend the Constitution but cannot change its "basic structure", such as democracy and fundamental rights. An independent judiciary limited the power of Parliament to protect core democratic principles.

items.stem: Explain why voting is seen as a responsibility as well as a right.
items.answer: Democracy depends on citizens taking part; if few people vote, governments may represent only some groups and lose legitimacy.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Democracy depends on citizens taking part; if few people vote, governments may represent only some groups and lose legitimacy. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why India adopted universal adult franchise from its first general election in 1951–52.
items.answer: The framers believed every citizen should have an equal political voice regardless of caste, gender, religion, wealth or literacy, to build a democracy that included the poor and historically excluded groups.
items.markingKey: Content: The framers believed every citizen should have an equal political voice regardless of caste, gender, religion, wealth or literacy, to build a democracy that included the poor and historically excluded groups. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. items.stem: The number of children of primary-school age out of school worldwide was 105 million in 2000 and 59 million in 2019 (UNESCO Institute for Statistics, approx.). Calculate the percentage change.
items.markingKey: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100 (M1) = (59 − 105) ÷ 105 × 100 = −43.8% (A1). Dividing by the new value is a common error.

items.stem:
Source A – Speech to the Constituent Assembly (paraphrased): Paraphrase of B. R. Ambedkar's speech to the Constituent Assembly, 25 November 1949

The speaker warned that on 26 January 1950 India would enter a life of contradictions: in politics there would be equality – one person, one vote, one value – but in social and economic life there would still be inequality. He urged that these contradictions be removed as soon as possible, or democracy itself would be put in danger.

Outline the main argument or view that Source A presents, quoting or referring to the source.
items.answer: Political equality will not last unless social and economic inequality is reduced.
items.markingKey: Political equality will not last unless social and economic inequality is reduced. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is too broad and theoretical for an investigation with evidence); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How do the rules made by our student council reflect the principles of democracy and the rule of law?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Young people should be given the right to vote at 16."
items.answer: Thesis: There is a reasonable case for voting at 16 if it is supported by strong citizenship education, as experience in Austria and Scotland suggests.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: 16-year-olds can work, pay taxes and are affected by long-term decisions such as climate policy; Austria, Brazil and Scotland (local and Scottish elections) allow voting at 16 or 17. Counter-arguments: many may lack experience of politics; they may be more easily influenced by parents or social media. Thesis/conclusion: There is a reasonable case for voting at 16 if it is supported by strong citizenship education, as experience in Austria and Scotland suggests. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem:
Source A – Speech to the Constituent Assembly (paraphrased): Paraphrase of B. R. Ambedkar's speech to the Constituent Assembly, 25 November 1949

The speaker warned that on 26 January 1950 India would enter a life of contradictions: in politics there would be equality – one person, one vote, one value – but in social and economic life there would still be inequality. He urged that these contradictions be removed as soon as possible, or democracy itself would be put in danger.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "India's constitution has been successful in protecting democracy."
items.answer: Largely successful: democratic institutions have survived and adapted, though the Emergency and ongoing inequality show that rights depend on vigilant citizens and courts.
items.markingKey: From the source: Political equality will not last unless social and economic inequality is reduced. Own knowledge for: regular elections and peaceful transfers of power since 1952; courts have protected the basic structure and rights. Own knowledge against: the Emergency of 1975–77 suspended rights and elections; inequalities of caste, gender and wealth still limit real equality. Judgement: Largely successful: democratic institutions have survived and adapted, though the Emergency and ongoing inequality show that rights depend on vigilant citizens and courts. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Democracy is always the best form of government."
items.answer: Thesis: Democracy is the system most likely to protect rights and accountability, but it works well only with the rule of law, protected minorities and informed citizens.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it protects rights and lets citizens remove leaders peacefully; leaders are accountable through elections and free media. Counter-arguments: decisions can be slow and short-term; majorities can ignore minorities if rights are not protected. Thesis/conclusion: Democracy is the system most likely to protect rights and accountability, but it works well only with the rule of law, protected minorities and informed citizens. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Who chaired the drafting committee of the Indian Constitution?
items.answer: B. R. Ambedkar
items.markingKey: C. He is often called the chief architect of the Constitution.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "separation of powers"?
options: Dividing government into legislature, executive and judiciary so that no one branch has too much power
The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted in 1989, which sets out the rights of everyone under 18
The idea that people have rights and responsibilities towards the whole world community, not only their own country
A system in which a hereditary monarch is head of state but power is limited by a constitution and an elected parliament
items.answer: Dividing government into legislature, executive and judiciary so that no one branch has too much power
items.markingKey: A. "separation of powers" is dividing government into legislature, executive and judiciary so that no one branch has too much power.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A freedom or entitlement that every person should have, protected by law"?
items.answer: right
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of right.

items.stem: Ana writes: "Fundamental Rights are unlimited." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They are subject to reasonable restrictions, for example free speech can be limited in the interests of public order, decency or the security of the state.
items.markingKey: They are subject to reasonable restrictions, for example free speech can be limited in the interests of public order, decency or the security of the state. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between direct democracy and representative democracy.
items.answer: In direct democracy citizens vote on laws themselves (Athens, Swiss referendums); in representative democracy they elect politicians to make laws for them (India, Canada).
items.markingKey: In direct democracy citizens vote on laws themselves (Athens, Swiss referendums); in representative democracy they elect politicians to make laws for them (India, Canada). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a moral right and a legal right.
items.answer: A legal right is written in law and enforceable by courts; a moral right is what people believe everyone should have, even if a law does not yet protect it.
items.markingKey: A legal right is written in law and enforceable by courts; a moral right is what people believe everyone should have, even if a law does not yet protect it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Freya writes: "Laws and rules are the same thing." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Rules can be set by any group (a school, a club); laws are made by the state and enforced by courts and police.

items.stem: Explain why children need their own rights convention in addition to general human rights.
items.answer: Children are more vulnerable, depend on adults and have special needs such as education, play and protection from exploitation, so the UNCRC sets out rights specific to childhood.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Children are more vulnerable, depend on adults and have special needs such as education, play and protection from exploitation, so the UNCRC sets out rights specific to childhood. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
A small country elects 10 seats, one per district, using first past the post. Results:
District 1: Liberals 4,600, Labour 3,400, Progressives 4,400
District 2: Liberals 5,300, Labour 5,000, Progressives 5,700
District 3: Liberals 2,800, Labour 3,600, Progressives 4,600
District 4: Liberals 5,200, Labour 2,200, Progressives 4,700
District 5: Liberals 3,600, Labour 2,800, Progressives 4,100
District 6: Liberals 4,200, Labour 2,500, Progressives 4,300
District 7: Liberals 2,400, Labour 3,600, Progressives 3,300
District 8: Liberals 4,800, Labour 2,800, Progressives 5,200
District 9: Liberals 2,200, Labour 4,400, Progressives 5,400
District 10: Liberals 4,000, Labour 2,000, Progressives 2,500
(a) How many seats does each party win? (b) Calculate each party's share of the total vote. (c) How many seats would each party get under proportional representation (largest remainder)? (d) Comment on the difference.
items.answer: FPTP: Liberals 3, Labour 1, Progressives 6; vote share: Liberals 33.8%, Labour 27.9%, Progressives 38.2%; PR: Liberals 3, Labour 3, Progressives 4
items.markingKey: (a) winner = most votes in each district (A1). (b) totals Liberals 39,100, Labour 32,300, Progressives 44,200 of 115,600 (M1 A1). (c) quota = share × 10; whole parts then largest remainders (A1). (d) FPTP can over-reward the party that wins many districts narrowly and under-represent parties whose votes are spread out; PR matches seats more closely to votes (R2).

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why an independent judiciary is important for the rule of law.
items.answer: Judges who cannot be dismissed by politicians can apply the law fairly, even against the government, so no one is above the law.
items.markingKey: Content: Judges who cannot be dismissed by politicians can apply the law fairly, even against the government, so no one is above the law. items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How do the rules made by our student council reflect the principles of democracy and the rule of law?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Read the council constitution and minutes; interview two council members and a teacher; survey 30 students; compare with criteria for democracy; record findings; evaluate bias in interviews.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Read the council constitution and minutes; interview two council members and a teacher; survey 30 students; compare with criteria for democracy; record findings; evaluate bias in interviews. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results.
